title: British Dort judgment on David and Peter: justifying faith can cease for a time
source_text: XLI. Profecto istud de Davide & aliis sanctis similiter lapsis expresse docent & affirmant Theologi Magnae Britanniae, in suo judicio circa quintum Remonstrantium articulum, quod actis Dordracenae Synodi insertum est. Ubi exemplis Petri & Davidis probant regenitos ac justificatos quandoque suo vitio in atrocia peccata incidere, & iis damnabilem reatum contrahere, & eorum merito, secundum Dei ordinationem, morti aeternae subjacere, & praesentem ad regnum coelorum ingrediendum aptitudinem amittere. Et consequenter affirmant, quanquam certum fuerit electos Dei servos Davidem & Petrum ad regnum coelorum perventuros, propter Dei electionem; tamen non minus certum esse, quod si ille in adulterio & homicidio, hic in Christi abnegatione & perjurio impoenitentes fuissent a morte deprehensi, neuter eorum salvus esse potuisset. Quibus subjungunt hanc Thesin, In illo interstitio, quod est inter contractum, ab homine, scilicet, electo & justificato, ex gravi peccato reatum, & fidei ac poenitentiae actum renovatum, stat talis peccator suo merito damnandus, Christi merito & firmo proposito absolvendus: non prius autem, quam per excitatam fidem ac poenitentiam veniam impetraverit, actu absolutus. Ex quibus aperte sequitur, juxta Theologos illos, fidem quae jam justificat, & per charitatem operatur, posse a charitatis operibus, quae sunt ad salutem necessaria, separari, & sic etiam ab actu justificandi cessare, & relinquere illum in quo inest damnationi aeternae obnoxium, pro illo tempore.
pass_a_gloss: Indeed the Theologians of Great Britain expressly teach and affirm this concerning David and other similarly fallen saints in their judgment on the Remonstrants' fifth article, inserted in the acts of the Synod of Dort. There by the examples of Peter and David they prove that the regenerate and justified sometimes by their own fault fall into atrocious sins, and contract damnable guilt by them, and by their desert according to God's ordination are subject to eternal death, and lose present fitness for entering the kingdom of heaven. And consequently they affirm that although it was certain God's elect servants David and Peter would reach the kingdom of heaven because of God's election, yet it is no less certain that if the one in adultery and homicide, the other in denial of Christ and perjury, had been overtaken by death impenitent, neither of them could have been saved. To which they subjoin this thesis: In that interval which is between the contracting of guilt from grave sin by an elect and justified man and the renewed act of faith and repentance, such a sinner stands by his own desert to be damned, by Christ's merit and firm purpose to be absolved: but not before, until through excited faith and repentance he has obtained pardon, is he actually absolved. From which it openly follows, according to those Theologians, that faith which already justifies and works through charity can be separated from charity's works necessary for salvation, and so also cease from the act of justifying, and leave him in whom it is liable to eternal damnation, for that time.
pass_b_english: British Dort theologians: regenerate David and Peter could fall into damnable guilt and lose present fitness for heaven.

Election made their final salvation certain; yet if death had taken them impenitent in those sins, neither could have been saved — justifying faith can cease for the interval before renewed repentance.
